Tip for anyone on UC: If you pay into a SIPP, you can report your net monthly pension contributions via your UC Journal. Pension payments reduce the assessed earned income, which lowers the income taper (as the taper rate is 55p in the pound on earnings above any work allowance). This means you can potentially get up to 55% of your net contribution back in extra UC, in addition to building up the pension pot. To claim it, report the net amount paid each month via the journal and upload screenshots showing the money leaving your bank account and arriving in your SIPP provider account as required.

You presumably still need money at the age you can draw your pension, so splitting contributions between accounts you can access earlier and the pension is the best of both worlds.

​@t-bodebates7119SIPPs were previously excluded from inheritance tax and so were used by some as a vehicle to pass on wealth. This was changed by reeves and now SIPPs will be included in iht rules. The problem is any money drawn from a SIPP is counted as income, so someone inherit a SIPP now they lose 40% straight away, then if working as most are, lose another 40% as they draw it so effective rate 73% essentially the state is taking most of a lifetimes worth of savings. So these people with large SIPPs used as wealth transfer mechanism for their family have begun taking out life insurance in trust so that when they die the life insurer essentially covers the 40% inheritance taxes and this sum being in trust is not included in the estate for iht purposes. A policy for a 50 year old insuring until 80 in trust can be under a thousand a year so more than worth it if your SIPP is close to lifetime allowances.

​​@t-bodebates7119The value of the insurance does depend on how far above the tax-free IHT threshold you are because you only pay IHT above the tax-free amount. One of the major advantages is that the insurance (if paid into a trust) can then be used to pay the IHT bill, which is usually due before probate is granted and before property is sold, so the estate needs access to cash to pay IHT before anyone receives any cash from the deceased. This may be less of an issue if IHT can be paid directly to HMRC from a pension fund prior to probate being granted.
No, the insurance cannot be paid directly from the pension fund, so I think the solution would be to halt pension contributions in order to fund the insurance, if you are likely to exceed the IHT tax-free threshold and the lump sum allowance (LSA). It's possible, of course, that you live beyond 80, so lifetime insurance may be preferable but also, the IHT threshold is likely to increase at some point in the future (it could also be reduced). If you consume your pension fund at a faster rate than it grows, this would also reduce your IHT liability.

​​@HandsomeT-b8cI think there are some rounding errors here and it's very much a worst-case scenario that actually applies to very few people. Yes, 40% IHT must be paid on the value of the estate above the tax-free threshold, so that leaves 60% of the pension to beneficiaries (assuming that there's no IHT-free allowance remaining. Then, if the inheritance is taxed at the 45% Additional Rate of income tax (so the donor was already over age 75), the additional rate of tax must be paid on drawdown. That could be as high as 45% of 60% = 27%, so 67% (not 73%) of the original amount is taken in tax, leaving the beneficiaries with just 33% of the original amount. If the beneficiary is not already a higher-rate taxpayer, or if they are able to increase their own pension contributions from income, then this worst case scenario could be avoided. In order to do so, it may be beneficial to hold the pension with a provider that allows beneficiary drawdown, so that the inheritance can be received progressively, rather than as a single lump sum.
